title: In awe the wind blows
hook: in awe the wind blows and rivers run; only the Formless is without fear (Asa di Var, ang 464)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kudrat: power and nature in one word, running through all of it. Today a salok a little further on shows the whole creation moving in awe.

Every morning the sun comes up within a few minutes of when the tables say it will. Tides arrive on schedule. Rivers that ran downhill in your grandparents' time still run downhill. Nobody stands on the mountain telling the water where to go. Scientists call these patterns laws. Guru Nanak, looking at the same faithful river and punctual sun, reached for a word you might not expect. Not law. Bhau. Fear, or awe. And in one long salok he hears the entire universe living inside it.
screen: `THE SUN, ON SCHEDULE.` → `RIVERS STILL RUN DOWNHILL.` → `GURU NANAK'S WORD: BHAU.`

segments.voice: Bhau is the Punjabi word at the center of this salok on ang 464, and it's hard to put into English. It can mean fear. But in Gurbani it often means something closer to reverence: the trembling respect of someone at the edge of a canyon. Listen to how the salok builds. Bhai vich, in awe, the wind blows, always. In awe a hundred thousand rivers flow. In awe fire does its work. In awe the earth carries its load. In awe Indra, lord of the rains, goes about head-down. In awe the sun and the moon travel their endless miles. In awe stand the adepts and the gods, the warriors and the mighty heroes, and in awe the crowds of people come and go. Notice the pictures. Wind that never takes a day off. Rivers that never refuse. Fire that keeps burning as if under orders. Guru Nanak is describing faithfulness. Everything in creation keeps its place and does its job, because it moves within the One's hukam, the divine order. Bhau is what that looks like from the inside. Then the turn. Awe, the salok says, is written on every forehead: sun, river, god, warrior. Only one is without fear: the Formless, the One who is true. Tomorrow we stay with that line. For today, one thing. In Sikh teaching, this awe isn't meant to make a person small and frightened. Elsewhere Gurbani pairs bhau with bhaau, awe with love, and some Sikh teachers describe the right kind of awe as what keeps love honest. The wind doesn't blow out of terror. It blows because it knows where it belongs.
screen: `BHAU: FEAR, OR AWE.` · `WIND, RIVERS, FIRE, EARTH, SUN.` · `EVERYTHING KEEPS ITS PLACE.` · `ONLY THE FORMLESS IS WITHOUT FEAR.` · then, large: `IN AWE THE WIND BLOWS.`

segments.voice: Feel the air on your face, or your own breath, the small wind you carry everywhere, moving without being asked. This air has moved faithfully since long before you and will move long after; let a little of the salok's awe settle in. If you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.
Bhau, awe or fear: Guru Nanak's picture of a faithful creation, wind, rivers, fire, earth, sun and moon, all moving bhai vich, in awe, within the One's order.
Your line: everything in awe. The wind knows where it belongs. Day five hundred forty-three, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of awe in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and many know its refrain, bhai vich, in awe, from long listening in the gurdwara.

fork.setup: you're Guru Nanak, watching rivers that never stop running and a sun that never misses its rising. what word do you give it?
fork.reveal: bhai vich: in awe the wind blows, the rivers flow, the sun and moon travel. only the Formless is without fear.

original.note: Gurmukhi: in awe, in fear; the refrain that opens each line of the salok.

trapdoor: what you thought: the wind is scared of God.
what it means: everything in creation moves faithfully within the One's order; that faithfulness is bhau, awe.
what a scholar hears: bhau (awe) and bhaau (love) are paired in Gurbani; here the refrain bhai vich builds a whole cosmology of obedience.

chat.says: Gurbani talks about fear a lot. Does it want people scared all the time?
options: Here bhau is closer to reverence; Gurbani pairs it with love, like wind keeping its place.
Yes, the salok says only terror of punishment keeps people and planets in line.
No, it says awe is a weakness, and the faithful should feel no reverence at all.
chat.meaning: Bhau in Gurbani often means reverent awe, paired elsewhere with bhaau, love. The wind blows because it belongs, not from terror.

bhau.meaning: fear, or awe, a trembling reverence

Indra.meaning: lord of the rains in old Indian lore

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (bhai vich pavan vahai), Ang 464

notes: The salok is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the list (wind, a lakh of rivers, fire, earth, clouds/Indra, Dharamraj, sun and moon, siddhas, warriors, crowds coming and going) and that 'awe is written on every forehead' fairly renders 'sagliaa bhau likhiaa sir lekh'.
Indra is rendered as 'the clouds' for a general listener; confirm this is acceptable or name Indra.
The pairing of bhau and bhaau (awe and love) is stated generally ('elsewhere in Gurbani... often'); confirm.
The opening comparison to natural laws is the narrator's framing, not a claim about the salok.
